scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Blades on the Mountain Pass
This is Chholiya. 10th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Chholiya traces its lineage back more than a thousand years to the warring Kshatriya clans of the Kumaon hills, including the Katyuris and Khasas, during an era when alliances and marriages were sealed at the point of the sword.
When the Chand Dynasty rose in the 10th century, arriving Rajput lineages merged with local communities and adopted Pahari language and customs, establishing a lasting martial ethos.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: While rooted in martial pageantry, Chholiya possesses significant religious and apotropaic weight, particularly among Rajput communities.
Wedding processions were traditionally believed to be open targets for demons and malevolent spirits seeking to ruin human happiness.
By waving swords, engaging in mock battles, and sounding martial horns, Chholiya dancers actively purify the procession path, warding off demonic forces to protect the bride and groom.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment is provided by fourteen musicians playing traditional martial and regional instruments.
Percussion is driven by the dhol and damau, played by hereditary musicians called dholies.
Listen for the turi, nagphani, ransing, dhol.

A booming, warlike outdoor soundscape defined by the thunderous pairing of dhol and damau drums played by dholies, punctured by the piercing brass calls of the turi, ransing, and serpentine nagphani. Over this martial percussion, the wailing reed drone of the masakbeen bagpipe intertwines with high woodwind melodies of the nausuriya muruli and twin flutes.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear traditional Kumaoni warrior attire consisting of a chola over white churidar payajama, topped with a taanka headpiece.
Their faces are smeared with sandalwood paste, mirroring warriors sanctifying themselves for war.
Each dancer carries a steel tulwar sword and a round brass shield, accompanied by the nishana, a triangular red flag.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources mention historical groups rather than individual performers: the Chand Kings of the 10th century, the Katyuri kings, the Khasas, and the Rajput lineages who shaped Pahari culture, alongside hereditary dholie drummers who maintain the musical lineages.

The dance exists across multiple named regional and stylistic forms: Bisu nritya, Saranv (focused on mock duels), Rann Nritya ('war dance'), Sarankar, Veerangna, Depanshu, Chholiya Baja, Paitan Baja, and Shauka Shaili, which is native to the Johar region of Kumaon.
Historically passed through Rajput and Khas communities of the Central Himalayas alongside hereditary dholie percussionist castes.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Chholiya carries an apotropaic religious function: performed during wedding processions (barat/baryat), it is believed to actively protect the couple by warding off malevolent spirits and demons attracted to human happiness. Outsiders should respect its ceremonial protective role during marriage rituals.
